names.name: pit
names.said: 'The pit' is the brick or block box the coals go in, the room it sits in, and often the whole business: 'out back at the pit', 'the pit opens at ten'.

etymology.root: Old English pytt 'a hole in the ground, water hole, well, grave', a Germanic borrowing of Latin puteus 'well, pit, shaft'; the barbecue sense keeps the hole's name after the hole has become a box of brick or cinder block above ground, and then a gas cooker inside a building
etymology.first_attested: Old English (etymonline); the barbecue-pit sense is undated in the dictionaries consulted — Wiktionary lists two dozen senses of pit and none for barbecue
etymology.note: Wikipedia's article on pit barbecue says the word is applied across the 'barbecue belt' to an enclosed, above-ground pit; NCpedia says few commercial barbecue pits today are dug in the ground.

text.what: The place the cooking happens. First a trench in the ground filled with hardwood coals, the split hog on a rack above; then a wide, shallow container of cinder block, brick or steel above ground, still a pit; then, at many places, a gas cooker, still the pit. The word also names the room, the building — a pit house — and the restaurant, as in Backyard BBQ Pit or Dickey's Barbecue Pit. A smokehouse is a different building: a windowless outbuilding where hams and bacon are cured in cold smoke for weeks, not a place a meal is cooked.
text.story: Pit is a Germanic borrowing of Latin puteus, a well; in Old English a hole, a well, a grave and hell. The barbecue pit was that hole: Wikipedia's article on pit barbecue describes meat cooked buried below ground, an earth-oven practice of Indigenous peoples. The whole-hog article has the pit dug into the earth or built above it as a wide, shallow container, usually of cinder blocks, filled with charcoal burned down from wood in a fireplace or a burn barrel; the South Carolina Encyclopedia gives the traditional pit as an open pit fuelled by hardwood coals in a rectangular cement-block structure, the meat suspended above. NCpedia says few commercial pits today are dug in the ground; the whole-hog article says new restaurants mostly use gas-fired pits and many older ones have switched. At the Skylight Inn the pit crew makes its charcoal from oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside the pits. Ed Mitchell co-founded a Raleigh restaurant called The Pit. *Inference —* a word that survived the loss of the hole survived the loss of the fire: the pit is wherever the barbecue is made, and the name on the sign says so.

kin.as: the masonry pit, the first form above ground.
the cinder-block pit, the common whole-hog form: a rectangular cement-block structure with the meat above the coals.
the drum beside the pit where logs become the coals shovelled in.
what burns beside the pit to make its coals.
the pit's way of cooking: coals under the meat, the meat on a rack above.
the cooker that replaced the coals at many pits and kept the name.
the pig pickin's charcoal or propane cooker, homemade or custom-built: a pit on wheels.
the person; the word is built on this one.
a Durham restaurant named for the thing.
where the coals for the pits are burned down from oak and hickory in fireplaces beside them.
a Greenville, South Carolina pit that calls itself a smokehouse — the two words meet on the sign.
who co-founded The Pit in Raleigh and left it in 2011.

confusable_with.tell: A cooker is an appliance; a pit is a place. When a pit switches to gas the appliance sits inside the place and the sign does not change.
A pig cooker is towed to the party; a pit stays where it was built.

text.story.note: the ground pit from the Pit barbecue article; the block pit from the Whole hog article and the SC Encyclopedia; the last sentence is inference

names.said.note: usage; the restaurant names are Backyard BBQ Pit (cast list) and Dickey's Barbecue Pit (Barbecue in the United States article)

images.alt: Smoke hangs in the air among tall bare-trunked trees. In the middle of the frame a man in a dark hat and coat stands in profile beside a low line of banked earth with meat and burning wood on it; two people sit on the ground to his left. Further back, small figures move around tables in a clearing. Across the foreground run the low ridges of a dug trench and a band of white canvas laid flat on the grass. Sepia print mounted on card.
